items.readable_text:
Content:
A good example of a direct variation model is the distance an object travels when moving at a constant rate. In this case, the corresponding direct variation equation is

Content:
[MATH: d=vt,]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: d] is the total distance traveled by the object,
- [MATH: t] is the total time that the object has been traveling, and,
- [MATH: v] is the constant of proportionality, called the speed of the object.

Content:
For instance, if an object travels a distance of [MATH: 24\,\textrm m] in [MATH: 4] seconds, then we can substitute [MATH: d=24\,\textrm m] and [MATH: t=4\,\textrm s] into the above equation and solve for [MATH: v,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 24|= v ⋅ 4; (24)/(4)|= v; 6|= v]

Content:
So, the equation that relates [MATH: d] and [MATH: t] is
[MATH: d=6t.]

Content:
One thing to note is that the constant of proportionality [MATH: v = 6] also has units. So let's work out what these units are.

Content:
Since we have

Content:
[MATH: d = vt,]
it follows that
[MATH: v = \dfrac{d}{t}.]

Content:
So, the units of [MATH: v] are

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm m}{\textrm s} = \textrm m / \textrm s.]

Content:
Therefore, the constant of proportionality (including its unit) is [MATH: v = 6\, \textrm m / \textrm s.]

sections.normalized_html: The force [MATH: F,] measured in [MATH: \text{kg}\, \text m / \text s^2], applied to a motorcycle varies directly with its acceleration [MATH: a,] measured in [MATH: \textrm{m}/\textrm{s}^2.] When the acceleration of the motorcycle is [MATH: a=5\,\textrm{m}/\textrm{s}^2,] the force is [MATH: F=2\,000\,\text{kg}\, \text m / \text s^2.] What is the constant of variation?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The force [MATH: F] is directly proportional to the acceleration [MATH: a,] so we have

[MATH: F = k{a},]

where [MATH: k] is the constant of variation.

We are told that when the acceleration is [MATH: a=5\, \textrm{m}/\,\textrm{s}^2,] the force is [MATH: F=2\,000\,\text{kg}\, \text m / \text s^2.] We can use this information to solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 2000|= k ⋅ (5); 2000|= 5k; (2000)/(5)|= k; 400|= k]

Finally, since [MATH: k = \dfrac{F}{a},] we have that the units of [MATH: k] are

[MATH: (kg m/s^{2})/(m/s^{2})|= (kgm/s^{2})/(m/s^{2}); = kg.]

Therefore, our final answer is [MATH: k = 400\,\textrm{kg}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The stretch [MATH: s] is directly proportional to the load [MATH: l,] so we have

[MATH: s = k{l},] where [MATH: k] is the constant of variation.

We are told that when [MATH: l=8\,\mathrm{g},] we have [MATH: s=9.6\,\mathrm{cm}.] We can use this information to solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 9.6|= k ⋅ (8); 9.6|= 8k; (9.6)/(8)|= k; 1.2|= k]

We now have the equation

[MATH: s = 1.2l.]

We can use this equation to find the load when the stretch is [MATH: s=7.2\,\mathrm{cm},] as follows:

[MATH: l|= (s)/(1.2); = (7.2)/(1.2); = 6]

Therefore, the load when [MATH: s=7.2\,\mathrm{cm}] is [MATH: l=6 \,\textrm{g}.]

The force [MATH: F] is directly proportional to the acceleration [MATH: a,] so we have

We are told that when the acceleration is [MATH: a=5\, \textrm{m}/\,\textrm{s}^2,] the force is [MATH: F=2\,000\,\text{kg}\, \text m / \text s^2.] We can use this information to solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 2000|= k ⋅ (5); 2000|= 5k; (2000)/(5)|= k; 400|= k]

Finally, since [MATH: k = \dfrac{F}{a},] we have that the units of [MATH: k] are

[MATH: (kg m/s^{2})/(m/s^{2})|= (kgm/s^{2})/(m/s^{2}); = kg.]

Therefore, our final answer is [MATH: k = 400\,\textrm{kg}.]

Content:

Explanation:
The stretch [MATH: s] is directly proportional to the load [MATH: l,] so we have

where [MATH: k] is the constant of variation.

We are told that when [MATH: l=8\,\mathrm{g},] we have [MATH: s=9.6\,\mathrm{cm}.] We can use this information to solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: 9.6|= k ⋅ (8); 9.6|= 8k; (9.6)/(8)|= k; 1.2|= k]

We now have the equation

[MATH: s = 1.2l.]

We can use this equation to find the load when the stretch is [MATH: s=7.2\,\mathrm{cm},] as follows:

[MATH: l|= (s)/(1.2); = (7.2)/(1.2); = 6]

Therefore, the load when [MATH: s=7.2\,\mathrm{cm}] is [MATH: l=6 \,\textrm{g}.]
